slides.title: Sullam Vocational Training Fund wants to offer support early
slides.text: The case study Sullam Vocational Training Fund wants to offer support early The fund A fictional fund that pays for programmes at 60 providers in 13 regions. 45,000 synthetic enrolments, 30,000 trainees, cohorts 2021 to 2025. The problem One enrolment in six ends without completion. A lost place costs SAR 9,000. The advisers can run 800 support plans a year. The model Mubakkir ranks trainees at the end of week 2 by the risk of not completing. You are Razan Al-Angari, the data scientist who builds it and defends its numbers. Synthetic, and treated as personal data. No row describes a real person or provider. Every lab handles the table as if it did.

slides.title: The two errors do not cost the same
slides.text: Two ways to be wrong The two errors do not cost the same Error What happens Cost to the fund Missed non-completer Nobody called; the place is lost SAR 9,000 Needless support plan An adviser's time went to a trainee who would have completed SAR 450 Support is not a cure One supported non-completer in four then completes (the advisers' own figure). Break-even A plan pays when p × 0.25 × 9,000 > 450: when the probability of not completing is above 0.20.

slides.title: Capacity turns a probability into a list of 800 names
slides.text: The action has a size Capacity turns a probability into a list of 800 names 8 in 100 scorable enrolments can get a support plan in the largest cohort: 800 plans for 10,100. Smaller cohorts, from 6,800, reach 12 in 100; the run log scores the top 8% The advisers do not ask "who is above 0.5?" They ask "which 800 first?" So the course scores rankings: average precision, and the share of non-completers on the list Accuracy is never reported

slides.title: A linear model is the first model worth beating
slides.text: Rung 3 A linear model is the first model worth beating Logistic regression: a weighted sum of the inputs, turned into a probability Its probabilities are usually close to observed rates Each weight can be read, with care On tables with mostly additive effects it is hard to beat by much What it cannot do alone It adds effects. "Absence matters, except for employer-sponsored trainees" is an interaction: someone has to write it in, or a tree has to find it. That is Day 2.

slides.title: A pipeline fits every preparation step on training rows only
slides.text: Preparation is part of the model A pipeline fits every preparation step on training rows only Impute Median, plus a "was missing" column → Encode One column per category; rare ones share one → Scale Mean 0, spread 1 → Model Logistic regression In each fold, fit sees the training rows; the validation rows only pass through transform 15 columns become 101 model inputs The entry test is missing for 14.2% of rows, and not at random: walk-in registrations skip it

slides.title: The whole rung is one object that can be fitted and scored
slides.text: In code The whole rung is one object that can be fitted and scored numeric = Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=True)), ("scale", StandardScaler())]) categories = Pipeline([("fill", SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="not recorded")), ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist", min_frequency=30, sparse_output=False))]) prepare = ColumnTransformer([("num", numeric, NUM), ("cat", categories, CAT)]) model = Pipeline([("prepare", prepare), ("model", LogisticRegression(C=0.1, max_iter=2000))]) One object, one rule. Whatever is inside the pipeline is refitted in every fold. Whatever you compute before it has seen every row.

slides.title: The logistic model wins on every fold, by far more than the spread

slides.title: The harm of preparing outside the folds depends on what the step has read
slides.text: What the pipeline protects The harm of preparing outside the folds depends on what the step has read Preparation Mean score Verdict Imputer and scaler inside each fold 0.5013 the reference Imputer and scaler fitted on all rows 0.5014 wrong, and almost free Provider rate from training rows 0.5018 honest Provider rate from all rows 0.5041 the gain is false What goes wrong. A step that never sees the outcome leaks little. A step built from the outcome (a rate per provider, a feature selection, a tuned setting) leaks in proportion to what it read.

slides.title: The time-travel test hides the future and checks that nothing changes
slides.text: A test, not a promise The time-travel test hides the future and checks that nothing changes 1 · Pick a past date For example 1 March 2023 → 2 · Compute twice From all records, and from the records ended by that date → 3 · Compare For every row predicted before that date A feature that reads the past only gives the same value both times The "started earlier" version changes for about 90 rows at each date: it fails The test checks the features, not the model, and takes seconds

slides.title: Gradient-boosted trees
slides.text: Session 1 Gradient-boosted trees Describe how boosting adds small trees to correct the errors so far Compare training and validation scores and read the gap Read importance scores and name two of their limits 01

slides.title: A tree splits the trainees into groups and predicts each group's rate
slides.text: The building block A tree splits the trainees into groups and predicts each group's rate Absent 2 days or more? The first question splits all trainees → Sponsored by an employer? Asked only inside the "absent" group → A leaf The share that did not complete among the trainees who land here Every question is "is this column above or below a value?" A second question inside one branch is an interaction, found without anyone writing it Scaling changes nothing: trees only compare

slides.title: Boosting adds one small tree at a time, each correcting the sum so far
slides.text: Many small trees Boosting adds one small tree at a time, each correcting the sum so far Start from the base rate Fit a small tree to what the current model still gets wrong Add a fraction of it: the learning rate Repeat a few hundred times The prediction is the sum of all the trees Why it leads on tables It handles mixed columns, missing values and interactions with little preparation, and it runs on a laptop processor. On medium-sized tables, tuned tree ensembles have matched or beaten deep networks in published comparisons.

slides.title: Defaults are one setting among thousands, chosen for nobody's table
slides.text: What ships in the box Defaults are one setting among thousands, chosen for nobody's table Setting LightGBM default What it controls Trees 100 How long the sum grows Leaves per tree 31 How many interactions one tree can hold Learning rate 0.1 How much each tree may correct Rows per leaf, at least 20 How small a group may be 31 leaves with 20 rows each. A tree may isolate a group of 20 trainees. With 9,000 training rows and a 12% outcome, that is two or three non-completers per leaf.

slides.title: A few settings trade flexibility against stability
slides.text: What to tune A few settings trade flexibility against stability How much is learnt The number of trees and the learning rate. They work as a pair: a smaller rate needs more trees. How complex each tree is Leaves per tree, and the fewest rows a leaf may hold. Fewer leaves and larger leaves: less to memorise. How much is held back Each tree sees a share of the rows and of the inputs; a penalty shrinks the leaf values. Lab 2.2 searches seven settings with 2,592 combinations. The budget is 20 of them.

slides.title: State the budget before the search, and draw the trials at random
slides.text: The rule State the budget before the search, and draw the trials at random A budget: 20 trials, fixed in advance, with a seed Random search : each trial draws every setting independently With a few settings that matter and several that hardly do, random draws cover the important ones better than a grid Every trial is kept, the poor ones too Why a budget is about honesty Each trial is another look at the validation rows. A search that stops "when the score looks good" has no defined number of looks, and its best score cannot be interpreted.

slides.title: One automates the search; the other arrives already trained
slides.text: Two kinds of challenger One automates the search; the other arrives already trained Automated machine learning You give the training rows, a metric and a time limit. The tool prepares the columns, trains several model families, tunes them and blends the best. Example: AutoGluon Tabular. It trains on your machine, on your rows only. A tabular foundation model A network pretrained on millions of synthetic tables. It reads your training rows as context and predicts the new rows in one pass, with no tuning. Example: TabPFN. Published results are strongest on small tables. Both are challengers, not shortcuts. Each has to stand on the same folds as the champion, in the same log.

slides.title: Two models on the same folds give pairs, and pairs are compared by their differences
slides.text: The key idea Two models on the same folds give pairs, and pairs are compared by their differences Spread of the champion's folds 0.012 Spread of the challenger's folds 0.017 Spread of the five differences 0.009 A hard half-year lowers both models The difference within a fold removes that shared part So the differences vary less than either score Compare two means with their spreads and you throw the pairing away

slides.title: Five differences give an honest, wide interval
slides.text: An interval on the mean difference Five differences give an honest, wide interval −0.007 mean difference, challenger minus champion; 95% interval −0.018 to +0.004 Mean ± t × (spread of the differences ÷ √5) With 5 folds the multiplier is 2.78, not 1.96 The interval contains zero: no difference is shown The folds share training rows, so the true uncertainty is, if anything, larger

slides.title: The paired bootstrap resamples validation rows, not folds
slides.text: A second opinion The paired bootstrap resamples validation rows, not folds Both models scored the same 21,770 validation rows Draw rows again with replacement, inside each fold Score both models on the same draw Keep the difference; repeat 1,000 times Method 95% interval of the difference t over five folds −0.018 to +0.004 Paired bootstrap over rows −0.013 to −0.002 Two questions. The first asks what other half-years would show, the second what other trainees in these half-years would show. Report both when they differ.

slides.title: State the smallest gain worth having before you look
slides.text: The decision rule State the smallest gain worth having before you look Adopt the challenger The whole interval lies above the minimum effect. Keep the champion The whole interval lies below the minimum effect. Not shown The interval straddles it. The rule says what happens then: the simpler model stays. For the fund: +0.01 average precision, agreed with Dr. Haya Al-Mogren before the contest.

Minimum effect stated in advance: +0.01. Decision: keep the champion. slides.title: A validation split is a rehearsal of how the model will be used
slides.text: The principle A validation split is a rehearsal of how the model will be used Who is new in use? New rows of known people, or people the model has never seen? If people are new, they must be new in validation. What is later in use? The model is trained once and scores what comes afterwards. Then validation rows come after training rows. What is known on that day? An outcome that does not exist yet cannot train a model. Training rows are those whose outcome was known. The split is chosen from the use, before any score is seen.

slides.title: Random, grouped and time-ordered splits answer different questions
slides.text: Three ways to cut the same rows Random, grouped and time-ordered splits answer different questions Split How it cuts The question it answers Random Each row lands in a fold by chance How well does the model do on more rows like these, from the same period? Grouped All rows of one trainee stay on one side How well does it do on a trainee it has never seen? Time-ordered Train on the past, validate on a later half-year How well does it do on the next intake? None is wrong in itself. A split is wrong for a use. A random split is right when rows are independent and the model is used on rows like them.

The whole class enters together, or not at all.

A world that moves fast Prices, fraud patterns, policies. The faster the change, the more a model's age costs. The habit. Choose the split from the use. slides.title: Kinds of leakage
slides.text: Session 2 Kinds of leakage Distinguish target leakage, future information, group or duplicate contamination and preparation leakage Identify the kind of leak from a description of how the data were collected Match each case to the validation scheme its use requires 02

slides.title: Leakage comes in four kinds
slides.text: A taxonomy Leakage comes in four kinds Target leakage A column written because of the outcome, or together with it. Future information A value computed from records later than the prediction time. Group or duplicate contamination The same person, machine or row on both sides of the split. Preparation leakage A step fitted or chosen on rows that later score the model. All four give a score in validation that the model cannot repeat in use.

slides.title: Target leakage: the column knows the answer
slides.text: Kind 1 Target leakage: the column knows the answer Recorded when the outcome happens: exit_reason, weeks_attended A consequence of the outcome: a cancellation fee, in a table that predicts which bookings are cancelled Someone's answer to the same question: a specialist referral written because the doctor suspects the condition The question When is this column written, and by whom? Would a person who already knew the outcome be the one filling it in? What goes wrong. The model looks brilliant and the top feature is one nobody questioned because it "obviously matters".

slides.title: Future information: right column, wrong date
slides.text: Kind 2 Future information: right column, wrong date A history that counts later records: all non-completions of a trainee, whenever they happened A yearly average attached to a row from March A status column overwritten in place: today's value on an old row The question On the day of the prediction, what would the value of this feature have been? Rebuild it with later records hidden and compare.

slides.title: Group or duplicate contamination: the model has met the test rows
slides.text: Kind 3 Group or duplicate contamination: the model has met the test rows Many rows of one unit, split at random: hours of one pump, visits of one patient The same record under two keys after two systems were merged Copies made on purpose: classes "balanced" by duplicating rows before the split The question What is the unit the model meets in use? Can the same real-world event appear in the table more than once?

slides.title: Preparation leakage: something was fitted before the split
slides.text: Kind 4 Preparation leakage: something was fitted before the split Scaling or imputing with statistics of all rows Encoding a category by its outcome rate over all rows Selecting the "best" features with the outcome of all rows Choosing settings on the rows that report the score The question Was any step fitted or chosen before the split? Everything that learns from data belongs inside the pipeline, fitted on training rows only.

slides.title: The validation scheme follows from the use
slides.text: The second half of each case The validation scheme follows from the use The model will be used on Scheme More independent rows like these, same period Random Units it has never seen: new pumps, new patients, a new site Grouped by that unit Later records of a population that changes Time-ordered New units, later Grouped and time-ordered In Lab 3.2 the last sentence of each case states the use.

slides.title: Three questions to any reported score
slides.text: Before any code Three questions to any reported score On which rows? How many test rows, from which period, with what share of the outcome? Do they look like the population the model will score? Against what? What does a constant answer score on the same rows? What did the previous model score? Chosen how? How many versions were tried, and on which rows was this one chosen? "95% accuracy" answers none of them.

slides.title: For a rare outcome, accuracy rewards saying "nothing happens"
slides.text: The metric For a rare outcome, accuracy rewards saying "nothing happens" "Everyone completes", all enrolments 0.83 "Everyone completes", scorable rows of 2024 H2 0.87 Loay's notebook, all five blocks repaired 0.89 Accuracy counts both classes alike and depends on their share It needs a threshold, and 0.5 is nobody's decision The run log uses average precision and recall at capacity for this reason

slides.title: Rows, split, preparation, tuning, metric
slides.text: An order to read in Rows, split, preparation, tuning, metric 1 · Rows Who is in the table? Anyone the model never scores? → 2 · Split Does it rehearse the use? → 3 · Preparation What was fitted, copied or encoded before the split? → 4 · Tuning On which rows was the model chosen? → 5 · Metric Does the number mean what the message says? The earlier the fault, the more of what follows it spoils.

slides.title: "Balancing the classes" before the split copies test rows into training
slides.text: The fault that did the damage "Balancing the classes" before the split copies test rows into training Each non-completer is copied four times, then the table is split at random Most test non-completers have a copy in training A tree with five rows per leaf recognises them The test set is half non-completers: no cohort looks like it If you balance at all Inside the training part only, as a step of the pipeline. The test rows keep the real share. Tomorrow shows that a ranking does not need it.

slides.title: A fixed threshold or a fixed list length
slides.text: The choice to write down A fixed threshold or a fixed list length Fixed list length Always fits the advisers. The weakest name on the list varies: in a hard intake, trainees at higher risk are left out. Fixed threshold Equal risk is treated equally across intakes. The list overruns or underuses capacity, and depends on the probabilities staying calibrated. Either can be defended; the fund chose the list length Write down which rule runs, and who may change it

slides.title: A calibrated score keeps a promise: of those given 0.3, three in ten leave
slides.text: The idea A calibrated score keeps a promise: of those given 0.3, three in ten leave Calibration is about what the numbers mean Ranking is about their order A model can be good at one and bad at the other It matters when the number is shown to an adviser, compared with a break-even, or multiplied by a cost How to measure it Sort the trainees by score and cut them into ten groups. In each: the mean score (expected) beside the share that left (observed). One summary number: the Brier score, the mean squared gap between score and outcome.

An adviser reads "0.90" beside a name. Of the trainees given that number, 55% left.

slides.title: A calibrator is a small model from score to probability
slides.text: The repair A calibrator is a small model from score to probability Sigmoid A logistic regression on the log-odds of the score: two numbers, a shift and a stretch. Works with few rows; cannot bend. Isotonic A rising step function. Takes any rising shape; needs more rows, and trainees on one step become tied. Fitted on rows the scoring model was not trained on: here the 2024 cohort Tested on rows neither has seen: the 2025 cohort For the weighted model the sigmoid's shift is −2.0; for the champion, −0.2

The sigmoid never changes the order; isotonic ties cost 0.03 here.

slides.title: Two errors, two different harms
slides.text: Errors are not symmetric Two errors, two different harms Missed A trainee leaves and was not on the list. Nobody called. The harm falls on the trainee. Measured among those who left: the miss rate, 0.62 for the 2025 list. Listed without need A trainee on the list would have completed anyway. An adviser's hour is spent; the trainee gets a friendly call. Measured on the list: one minus precision. The first harm leads the audit The question: is the miss rate the same for everyone?

slides.text: The tool A rate from a small slice needs an interval that knows its size Slice Left Missed 95% interval Riyadh 444 0.58 0.53 to 0.62 Jazan 86 0.73 0.63 to 0.82 Qassim 21 0.81 0.60 to 0.92 Al-Baha 12 0.75 0.47 to 0.91 The miss rate is a share of those who left: that count sets the width The Wilson interval stays inside 0 and 1 and behaves for small counts Read the width before the position

slides.title: By the rule stated in advance, two regional gaps are supported
slides.text: Lab 4.3, measured By the rule stated in advance, two regional gaps are supported The rule: a gap is supported when the whole interval lies above or below the cohort's miss rate, 0.62 Jazan: 0.73, interval 0.63 to 0.82: above Riyadh: 0.58, interval 0.530 to 0.622: below 0.623, by a hair Najran, 0.75: its interval starts at 0.61 Qassim, 0.81: too few cases to tell Nineteen slices Thirteen regions, two genders, four age bands. With that many, one can cross the line by chance. A rule fixed in advance limits the damage; a cause you can check does more.

slides.title: Leaving a column out does not make a model blind to it
slides.text: A common belief Leaving a column out does not make a model blind to it Gender is not a feature of Mubakkir Other features differ between women and men: programme, employment, distance And who is in the data differs: 43% against 52% So errors can still differ by gender What follows The attribute stays in the table, outside the model, so that errors can be audited. Under the Personal Data Protection Law personal data serve a stated purpose: here the audit of errors, agreed with the fund's data protection officer.

slides.title: A model card is the one page that travels with the model
slides.text: The hand-over A model card is the one page that travels with the model Measured: filled from results Intended use · data · validation scheme · results on held-out rows · calibration · errors by subgroup. Written: no number writes them What the model is not for · where the scores do not hold · who decides · what the next team needs. Its readers were not in the room: an adviser, an auditor, the deployment team Every number in it can be traced to a run

slides.title: The results section says what was not shown
slides.text: What the card admits The results section says what was not shown Champion 0.529 on the folds; against the logistic rung +0.005, interval −0.010 to +0.019: an advantage is not shown New trainees 0.491, returning trainees 0.578: the headline is an average Expected 13.7%, observed 13.5% overall; four points too low at new providers Why write it down. The next team may need a model an adviser can read, or one that is cheaper to run. The card tells them a simpler one does as well within the uncertainty.

slides.title: A useful limit names a situation and what to do in it
slides.text: The written half A useful limit names a situation and what to do in it Weak Useful "May not generalise to new data." "At a provider that opened after training the probabilities are about four points too low: use the rank, not the number." "Performance may degrade over time." "A model one year old scored 0.016 lower: retrain every half-year, on programmes due to end." "Use with care in some regions." "Where attendance is kept on paper, a trainee who is not on the list is not thereby low-risk." A reader should recognise the situation when they are in it.

slides.title: The score puts a name on a list; a person decides
slides.text: The sentence to keep The score puts a name on a list; a person decides An adviser decides whether and how to contact a trainee An adviser may add any trainee who is not on the list No trainee is refused, ranked for funding or told a score Providers are not ranked by it What the score does not answer It says who is likely to leave. It does not say whether a support plan helps, or whom it helps most. That needs a comparison of supported and unsupported trainees, which the fund has not run.
